title: Identifying and preventing vulnerabilities (part 1)
starter: Your school has £5,000 to spend on security. List what you would buy, in order, and say what each purchase protects against.
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Penetration testing
facts: Evaluating the security of a system by safely trying to exploit its weaknesses.
It's done with the owner's permission, and the findings are reported so they can be fixed.
Testers act like attackers, including trying social engineering.
stations.challenge: Write the definition of penetration testing in your own words.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Evaluating the security of a system by safely trying to exploit its weaknesses.
Also credit: It's done with the owner's permission, and the findings are reported so they can be fixed.

questions.a: Attacking a system with the owner's permission to find its weaknesses
The organisation has given permission for the tests

stations.name: Anti-malware software
facts: Scans files and programs and compares them against known malware.
Watches for suspicious behaviour to catch new threats.
Must be kept up to date, because new malware appears daily.
Quarantines or removes anything it finds.
stations.challenge: Why does anti-malware need updating so often?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Scans files and programs and compares them against known malware.
Also credit: Watches for suspicious behaviour to catch new threats.

questions.a: Detects, blocks and removes malicious software

questions.q: Why must anti-malware be updated regularly?
questions.a: New malware appears constantly, so it needs new definitions

stations.name: Firewalls
facts: A firewall controls the traffic entering and leaving a network.
It checks packets against a set of rules and blocks anything not allowed.
It can block suspicious ports, addresses and programs.
Firewalls can be hardware, software, or both.
stations.challenge: Explain the difference between a firewall and anti-malware software.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A firewall controls the traffic entering and leaving a network.
Also credit: It checks packets against a set of rules and blocks anything not allowed.

questions.a: Controls traffic entering and leaving a network using a set of rules

questions.q: Which attack does a firewall help most against?
questions.a: Unauthorised access attempts and suspicious traffic from outside

stations.name: User access levels
facts: Each user only gets access to what they need for their role.
Students, teachers and network managers have different rights.
If an account is compromised, the damage is limited to that user's access.
stations.challenge: Why shouldn't every teacher have network manager rights?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Each user only gets access to what they need for their role.
Also credit: Students, teachers and network managers have different rights.

questions.q: What are user access levels for?
questions.a: Limiting each user to the data and settings they need

questions.q: A student's account is stolen by an attacker. Why do access levels help?
questions.a: The attacker can only reach what a student can reach

stations.name: Monitoring and policies
facts: Network forensics means watching network traffic to detect intrusions and collect evidence.
An acceptable use policy is the set of rules a user signs up to before being allowed on the network.
Logs record who did what and when.
stations.challenge: Write three rules from your school's acceptable use policy.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Network forensics means watching network traffic to detect intrusions and collect evidence.
Also credit: An acceptable use policy is the set of rules a user signs up to before being allowed on the network.

questions.q: Match each term to its definition.
questions.a: Network forensics → Watching network traffic to spot intrusions and gather evidence about what happened; Penetration testing → Attacking a system with permission, to find its weaknesses before criminals do; Acceptable use policy → The rules a user signs up to before they are allowed on the network

stations.name: Which defence?
facts: Match the defence to the threat: anti-malware for malware, firewalls for unwanted traffic.
Access levels limit the damage when an account is compromised.
Penetration testing finds the gaps before attackers do.
stations.challenge: Which defence would you buy first for a small business, and why?
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Match the defence to the threat: anti-malware for malware, firewalls for unwanted traffic.
Also credit: Access levels limit the damage when an account is compromised.

questions.q: A company keeps getting infected by malware from downloads. Which helps most?
questions.a: Anti-malware software, kept up to date

questions.q: A company wants to find weaknesses before criminals do. What should it arrange?

final.name: Final challenge: defence definitions

questions.q: Match each prevention method to its description.
questions.a: Penetration testing → Attacking a system with permission, to find weaknesses before criminals do; Anti-malware software → Detects, blocks and removes malicious software; Firewall → Controls traffic entering and leaving a network using rules; User access levels → Limits each user to the data and settings their role needs; Network forensics → Monitors and analyses traffic to detect intrusions and gather evidence; Acceptable use policy → The rules a user signs up to before using the network

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: Describe what happens during a penetration test, and why organisations pay for one.
points: Penetration testing finds the gaps before attackers do.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Explain how a firewall reduces the risk of unauthorised access.
points: A firewall controls the traffic entering and leaving a network.
Each user only gets access to what they need for their role.
If an account is compromised, the damage is limited to that user's access.
Access levels limit the damage when an account is compromised.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

exam.q: Explain how user access levels limit the damage caused by a stolen password.
points: Access levels limit the damage when an account is compromised.
If an account is compromised, the damage is limited to that user's access.
Each user only gets access to what they need for their role.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 3.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
